This page provides a (relatively) tour of Starsim. It builds up a model step by step: a simple epidemic, then with age groups, an intervention, data to fit it to, and multiple runs with uncertainty.

To follow along, install Starsim with `pip install "starsim[jax]"`, then download this page as a Jupyter notebook from the "Jupyter notebook" link beside the page's contents. You can also clone the [Starsim repository](https://github.com/starsimhub/starsim) and open `docs/tour.qmd` in Jupyter (with `jupytext` installed, Jupyter opens `.qmd` files directly).

## An SIR model

Let's start with the standard SIR model. Everyone is in one of three compartments: susceptible (S), infectious (I), or recovered (R). The equations are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dS}{dt} &= -\beta \frac{S I}{N} \\
\frac{dI}{dt} &= \beta \frac{S I}{N} - \gamma I \\
\frac{dR}{dt} &= \gamma I
\end{aligned}
$$

where N = S + I + R is the population size. People change state via two *transitions*:

- **Infection**, from S to I. Each susceptible person is infected at a rate of β times the fraction of people who are infectious, so the number infected per day is β S I / N. Since the "S/N" is actually an approximation for how people in the population mix, which in Starsim you often specify explicitly (e.g. via a network), you can omit it.
- **Recovery**, from I to R. People stay infectious for 10 days on average, so they recover at a rate of γ = 1/10 per day.

In Starsim, the compartments are called *states*, and the transitions say where people move from, to, and at what rate (after `@`):

```{python}
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I        # From S to I, at a rate of 0.3 times the fraction infectious
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)  # From I to R, after 10 days on average
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery)
```

A state in a rate, like `I` in `0.3*I`, is the fraction of people in it. A duration, like `ss.days(10)`, is the average time spent in a state before leaving it. Since the duration is in days, β = 0.3 is per day. You can check what equations Starsim interpreted from what you gave it:

```{python}
sir.equations()
```

To run the model, put it in a sim and say how long to run it for:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(sir, dur=ss.days(100))
sim.run()
sim.sir.plot()
```

The sim says what it ran and some key results: 10,000 people (the default population) as an ODE, R0 = 3 as expected (=0.3/0.1), and the number of infections. Since nothing in this model is about individual people, Starsim runs it as a deterministic compartmental model (an ODE). The same model can also be run as a stochastic model or as agents, as [the last section](#uncertainty-and-many-runs) shows.

## Checking the model

Starsim has defaults for pretty much everything (all of which can of course be overridden). `describe()` lists the whole model as Starsim has built it: every state and transition, plus any parameters that used Starsim defaults:

```{python}
sim.describe()
```

## Age groups and contacts

Many diseases spread differently between age groups. `stratify()` splits each state into substates: here we split into three age groups. `ss.contacts()` says how the groups mix with each other: the entry in row *i* and column *j* is the number of contacts a day that people in *i* have with people in *j*. β is the rate of infection per contact. This model also has an outcome, `cases`, representing the infections that are reported.

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
beta = ss.par(0.02, bounds=[0.005, 0.1]) # A parameter that can be fitted, between these bounds
dur_inf = ss.par(ss.days(10))            # The mean infectious period

infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ dur_inf
cases     = ss.outcome(0.2*infection) # One infection in five is reported
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, cases, init_prev=0.0001)
sir.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the fraction of people in each

contacts = ss.contacts(
    ages=[0, 15, 65],
    matrix=[
        [18, 2, 1],
        [2, 4, 1],
        [1, 1, 5]]
)
pars = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=1e6, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01')
sim = ss.Sim(sir, **pars)
sim.run()
sim.results.sir.cases.by('age').plot()
```

Every state and transition has a result of the same name (`S`, `I`, `R`, `infection`, `recovery`), and so does each outcome (`cases`). `by('age')` splits a result by age group, and `select()` picks one group, e.g. `sim.results.sir.I.select(age='65+')`.

## Interventions

As was drilled into everyone's heads during the COVID pandemic, interventions can be pharmaceutical or non-pharmaceutical. Here we introduce one of each: masks, which cut everyone's transmission by 40%; and vaccinating 80% of children under 15 with a vaccine that cuts their chance of infection by 90%:

```{python}
masks = ss.modify(sir.pars.beta, multiply=0.6, start='2025-01-20')
vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, who=sir.age < 15, when='2025-01-20', coverage=0.8)
```

To compare them, make a sim for each scenario, and run them in parallel with `ss.parallel()`:

```{python}
scenarios = {'No intervention': None, 'Masks': masks, 'Vaccine': vaccination}
sims = {}
for label, intervention in scenarios.items():
    sims[label] = ss.Sim(sir, interventions=intervention, **pars)

msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sir.infection')
```

`msim.summarize()` gives each result over the whole run (the total of a flow, such as infections, and the final value of a state) for each scenario; here, the infections:

```{python}
msim.summarize('sir.infection')
```

Masks prevents about a third of infections, while vaccination prevents more than half.

## Data and fitting

A model is fitted by finding the values of its parameters that make its results match data. We can use our model to create synthetic data and then fit to it. Here we set β = 0.02, and draw weekly counts of cases from it, with random noise as in real reporting. Real data never come from exactly the model being fitted, so here set  the data come from a slightly different one, in which the infectious period varies less from person to person (an Erlang distribution with 3 stages, rather than the exponential of the model). The noise is drawn with the true sim's own random seed (`rand_seed=4`), and we use a stochastic solver (tau-leaping) rather than an ODE.

```{python}
truth = ss.Sim(sir, pars=dict(beta=0.02, dur_inf=ss.erlang(k=3, mean=ss.days(10))), rand_seed=4, solver='tau', **pars)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_synthetic_data('cases', resample='week', noise=ss.nbinom(n=5))
data.head()
```

A forecast is made from the data so far. Here, the first four weeks of cases, up to 1 February, are the data, and the sim stops when they do. Data is matched to results by name: the column `cases` is compared with the result `cases`, and since the data is weekly, each row is compared with the total of the model's cases over its week. `sim.fit()` then fits every parameter that has bounds (here, β) to every result that has data:

```{python}
early = data[data.date <= '2025-01-22']
sim = ss.Sim(sir, data=early, **(pars | dict(stop='2025-02-01')))
fit = sim.fit()
fit.plot()
```

The plot shows the model's cases with the starting value of β (before) and the fitted one (after), against the data. `fit.pars` has the values found:

```{python}
fit.pars
```

The fitted β is higher than the actual 0.02, since the fitted model's exponential infectious period gives a slower growth than the Erlang distribution.

`fit.project()` runs the fitted model on, here to 1 July, for the forecast; given all the data, its plot shows the cases that were still to come:

```{python}
forecast = fit.project(stop='2025-07-01', data=data)
forecast.plot('sir.cases')
```

From the first four weeks alone, the forecast gets the timing and size of the peak about right.

## Uncertainty and many runs

The ODE gives the maximum likelihood answer, but real epidemics also include stochastic variability, especially when there are a small number of cases. To see this, we run the fitted model in a population of 20,000 as a stochastic model, in which the number of people who move between states each day is random. We do this by setting `solver='binomial'` (short for [chain binomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reed%E2%80%93Frost_model)), and `n_runs=40` runs it 40 times, each with its own random seed:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(sir, pars=fit.pars, solver='binomial', **(pars | dict(total_pop=20_000)))
msim = ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=40)
msim.plot(['sir.I', 'sir.cases'], lines=True)
```

The plot shows each of the runs (omit `lines=True` to show the median and 95% range instead). The results are available as a dataframe via `msim.summarize()`:

```{python}
msim.summarize()
```

Nearly the same number of people are infected each time, but the epidemics vary considerably in terms of peak timing.
